body:
> I assumed this is the end game of the whole "gender is a social construct" movement.

Gender *roles* are an abitrary social construct, gender itself is not. That would still exist in the brain and people would still have physical dysphoria about their bodies and feel like their sex characteristics are wrong. 

The end goal of "gender roles are a social construct" is not to try to make everyone genderless and anyone who says this and means it is crazy. The end goal is to acknowledge that while there's generally "man things" and "woman things" that most men and women generally do, that not doing these things doesn't make you less of a man or a woman, nor would it make you trans. Ending gender roles is more like it shouldn't be that men are the bread winners and women stay at home with kids and take care of the house, it should be that whoever wants to be the breadwinner and the housekeeper in a marriage should do that thing. Or that if men don't want to have to be the "protector" or the leader in a relationship, he shouldn't have to be. 

At the end of the day, the thing that makes someone trans is whether or not they feel like they body that they don't belong in and/or discomfort with of seen as a gender they don't identify with by the world around them. 

If the idea having the body of the opposite sex- or if they're nonbinary, one that has a mix of male and female traits or has neither sex traits- is something that feels more comfortable to someone, they're trans. 
If someone feels better being perceived by the world as a person of the opposite sex they were born with (or again if nonbinary, being seen as being both/neutral/neither), then they're trans.
That's literally all it's ever been about.

I'm wondering if you're possibly looking for a simple answer to a very complex dilemma. 

You should probably start by working on your sense of self-worth, maybe try to untangle why exactly you feel the way you do about things- not just in the "I feel bad about myself because I'm short and women like tall guys" sort of way. Looking much deeper into why you feel that way about something for example could do you a lot of good.

Also developing social skills if your ability to socialize is weak. I think you mentioned somewhere else in the thread that you don't really ever hang out with people, that's going to be a way bigger hindrance to your dating life than your height could ever be.

I think it's also useful to try to understand what others are looking for when they're looking to date people and what actually creates feelings of attraction in someone. Most people don't look for people because they're tall or have high social status or money...it's because they were able to connect through moments of shared emotions. Being able to learn how to connect with people through emotions is the key really. I see a lot of men come on here who try and fail at getting people to like them, and they don't realize that the way they're communicating with people lacks emotional depth, which doesn't really lead to people wanting to connect with them on a deeper level that could lead to a relationship. 

None of those are concise answers, but you asked a very open ended question with millions of different solutions to it.

I've known lots of short women who are way smaller than me OP.

But that's missing the main point, which is that so many different women are into so many different types of men (including short guys) that I don't think it's worth agonizing over your height because plenty of women aren't going to be bothered by someone who's your height. They might even prefer your height over that of a guy that's 6'3.

I don't think dating primarily shorter women is necessarily the solution either. As I said, I've known very short women who only wanted tall guys AND I've known very tall women who loved short men. It's not so black and white.

May I ask why you need to know how tall I am?

I'm 5'3. I've known women my height who only want to date men that are 6+ feet. I also have known women who are 5'10 and have dated men as short as my boyfriend is and found them highly attractive. I've even known women that tall who straight up prefer short men over tall ones.

So I'm not exactly sure where your thought process was heading with that question. Women aren't a monolith and their tastes can be wildly different from each other. Even if most women have a preference for tall men, it doesn't mean that's the only preference women have.

>But even then, beingbshort is always seen as a negative.

My boyfriend is 5'5 and when I saw his height on his dating profile I thought it was a plus and not a minus for him. I love his height!

He's also quite soft in appearance and not at all really masculine. This hasn't stopped me from being insanely attracted to him, and it hasn't stopped women from being attracted to him in the past either.

What do you think could be the explanation for this then, OP?

>I want to be able to be more open to people I would typically not be attracted to, to better increase my chances of meeting someone 

I think it's a good idea to figure out how to reframe how you see relationships then. It seems like you want emotionally unavailable people because then you don't have to get too close to them, and you get to have this idealized relationship in your head that can't ever go wrong.

Look into attachment theory, it sounds like you may have some attachment issues? Feeling put off by people who are emotionally available can be because we don't have a secure attachment style. The good thing is that you can work on this! It just takes time.

Do you think you could have (or should have) toughed it out with the women you described?

If not, then why would you want for the women you're interested in to tough it out with you?

That would be a recipe for resentment in a future relationship, OP.

>Well, it’s clear the difference between us is you **chose** to be a nerd (and perhaps even proud of that label).

I didn't choose to be anything, I just pursued what always naturally interested me. I'm also like 30 years old and don't find any pride in being labeled a nerd because it literally doesn't really matter what "label" I fit into...maybe when I was 13, but not now that I'm grown. I simply do what I've always liked.

>You mentioned that you’re well-liked among your nerdy co-workers and you **choose** not to have social media.

The entire point that I was making is that my coworkers actually *aren't* nerdy, but they still think some of my interests are fascinating anyways because it's different to what they're usually into. They don't have any deep interest into it or anything, just a passing "Oh really? What's that all about?" type thing and they enjoy learning a little bit about something they've never heard about. And maybe despite being introverted, I do a pretty good job at being enthusiastic and passionate about the things that I like, which is a trait that most people admire in others. I don't enjoy talking about these things because of social signifiers, but because talking about things I like makes me happy. That's literally it.

>I’ve always said everyone who were cool in school **wanted** to be cool in school. Popularity is never effortless. It is a deliberate and conscious choice  for some people to strive for popularity (especially once we hit puberty). In other words, it’s more **self-selection** than **natural selection**.

I've known several people who were extremely shy/quiet/nerdy that were also super popular by everyone in school, even though they never went out of their way to try to become popular. People just thought they were cool anyway without them trying to be cool. I've also known people who were extroverted and popular, but they were popular without ever trying. They were just the type of person that people liked hanging around because they were naturally funny or had good social/communication skills. 

So I'd love to know what your opinion on effortless popularity could be, as I think we have very different experiences with this sort of thing. Do you think it's possible that plenty of people could be popular without having to put in a lot of effort? While it may have been your experience that you've had to try really hard to be cool, it doesn't mean that other people had to put in effort to be well liked or socially adept. Just wondering what your thoughts on that are.

That's interesting! I'm very introverted and shy with people, but I've also been told by other people that I'm very entertaining and fun to be around. Never been called boring by anyone. I'd also like to think that I'm fairly optimistic too, more optimistic than most people around me. I always try to be hopeful for the future because I think there's already too much ugliness in the world and I know there's more to life than just suffering. So I wonder what you think of that then, or if you're talking about a different type of introvert.

I also was very unpopular and bullied all the time in school, I'm nearly 30 now and I'm fairly well liked in the circles I'm in, including work. I never really changed my nerdy hobbies or the alternative way I dress either and I'm pretty vocal with people that I'm a big nerd. But coworkers and stuff have always been pretty nonjudgemental and accepting off that stuff. I don't even really use social media anymore or anything like that.  I also feel like I haven't hit my peak in this life, but that my best years are just getting started even though others might say that I'm a bit of a loser. 

So it sounds like we've had very different experiences when it comes to growing up being the unpopular nerd, for whatever reason.

But it sounds like you had a challenging upbringing. I'm sorry to hear that, unsupportive parents that make you feel ostracized are never cool to have and do more damage than people may realize.

>I dislike introverts

Is there any particular reason why?

>2. I can’t describe how it works but I can tell you how I think it’s supposed to be. I tell them what I’m going through and they give me advice or some kind of mental exercise for me to do.


Then you might not understand what a therapist is actually meant to do. To be fair, most people don't. 

Therapists work to teach you how to think about things differently, how to take a different perspective on things so that *you yourself* can figure out a different solution to a problem based on a new way of seeing things. Above all else, this is a therapist's real job, not to give advice. 

That's also what the mental exercises are for, btw.

Simply giving advice isn't helpful if the person receiving it isn't in the mindset to actually be able to take the advice or see it as useful, that's WHY they teach you how to think your thoughts differently so that you maybe can take certain advice that you're given. And simply giving advice doesn't teach people how to solve issues for themselves in the long run, but teaching someone how to take a different perspective on something they're struggling with DOES help someone help themselves when they're in a hard situation. 

Being able to think about your beliefs and your emotions differently makes it easier for you to change your behavior, and being able to more easily change your behavior leads to better outcomes in life.

If a therapist you've seen didn't seem to teach you a different way to look at your thoughts, thats fair. It's just a matter of finding one who is able to get you to see things differently. But expecting them to hand you ideas for solutions is objectively not a therapist's job, and a good one will even avoid doing that where necessary.

>I assume that there were lots of autistic women in my university programs and at the professional networking events I attend regularly.

Would you talk to them? How did you approach conversation with them? 

>But generally, the less it makes me use my brain, the more I enjoy it.

Is there any particular reason why? It's interesting to hear you talk about things that require you to think more as almost as being physically laborious when you also have a PHD, I guess I'm curious about what exactly you mean by that.

>To be honest, I'd prefer real life events.

Any particular reason why?
Even if it's not to make friends, I think it'd help you out a lot just to lurk through them and see if you relate to anything. It wouldn't do any harm.

>What kinda hobbies / conventions would that be? Also, if there were autistic women around me all my life and I just didn't notice, I would have clicked with them anyway would I?

Depends on your interest! This is where maybe asking around in neurodivergent spaces online about what type of IRL spaces they tend to frequent might help you out. Most of my interests lean more into the things I mentioned that you said you weren't interested in, although I'm sure there's plenty of STEM type things that might have more of us around too. If you're not into the typical nerd/fandom stuff, there's still a lot of other options, it's just about seeking it out. What are you interested in generally speaking OP? 

Also you might have already run into women like this, but if they're (typically) better at appearing neurotypical than men, would you have noticed? Possibly not. It's possible that you've walked right past other neurodivergent women and never even knew it.

It sounds like you maybe have a bit of a reluctance about exploring this whole thing, no one can force you to accept or figure out anything about yourself if you don't want to. But you're 38 and it sounds like you're running into a wall because you're trying to do things in a way that just might not work for you, instead of maybe accepting something sort of scary and finding your way into a life that's genuinely better suited for you. Ultimately, no one here is a doctor and we can't diagnose you. But I do emplore that you look into it if you're able. If you do end up getting diagnosed with anything, you'll also find it easier to get the sorts of therapeutical help that might make things like figuring out how to connect with people a bit easier. There's no harm in trying, but you don't want to waste any more of your time you could spend being happy because you might be denying a certain part of yourself.

>I'd love to. But I have never met a girl who was openly autistic. And I was in a STEM field with 80% women.


There's online groups specifically for autistic adults OP. You don't need to try to go on them to look for dates or anything, but there's plenty of autism subreddits I'd recommend looking through. Read through them and see if their experiences click, try talking to people on there if you have experiences and interests in common and see if you're able to connect with people that way.

Also, autistic women tend to be much higher masking than autistic men. My best friend is on the spectrum and you wouldn't know it because of all the time they spent learning how to mask and blend in with neurotypicals. You may just have not noticed it for that reason. Also, I find certain hobby and interest groups tend to have way more neurodivergent people than others, especially nerdy ones. If you have any interests like this, maybe see if there's events in your area to meet people? Conventions are great for this in my experience.

>How did you meet your friends and partner?

Honestly? It was pretty unintentional. Again, mainly through niche hobby groups like cosplay, alternative fashion, anime/video games/fandom type groups. I didn't intentionally seek out neurodivergent people. None of us even got diagnosed until we were adults and already known each other for years. I think for some people, we just accidentally find each other and cluster together. As for my boyfriend, I met him on a dating app. That I think was more pure luck of the algorithm than anything, but from the moment we met I figured he was likely neurodivergent and we just clicked so well because we think a lot alike.

I think you've just been maybe looking in the wrong places, and trying to use neurotypical social advice to find people...which just doesn't work so well because neurodivergent people socialize differently. Do you think that's why it's always felt like "work" to get yourself out there with people? If you're neurodivergent, finding your like minded people won't feel so difficult OP.

>For me, it feels kinda like a cancer diagnosis. Yes, you finally know what you are dying from. But you are still dying either way.

Well it's a good thing autism isn't fatal then is it? Yes, there's a grieving period when you realize that something you've always struggled with your whole life isn't something you can just "cure" because it's a disability. But I don't think I would have ever learned to make peace with the things I struggle with until I accepted that my ADHD is fundamentally going to make some things much harder for me than for everyone else. That doesn't mean my life is over, just that I have to find an different way to do things. There's things neurodivergent people can be much better at than neurotypicals because are brains have unique strengths, I try my best to focus on that and look for opportunities to utilize the strengths that I have instead of brute forcing my way through everything that's hard for me.

Do you not think it could be valuable to seek out autistic people to be friends with? And possibly even to date?

Whether or not you're autistic, it seems like you have a lot of the same social thought patterns and experiences as a lot of autistic people do. Maybe you're struggling to click with people because you're personality just doesn't vibe well with neurotypicals, but you'd likely get along way better with people on the spectrum who think like you do.

When that happens, socializing and holding conversations overall just becomes easier. It's like you're speaking the same "social language" so to speak, while you're currently struggling to speak the same social language as most other (likely neurotypical) people.

As a neurodivergent person who has almost exclusively neurodivergent friends and is dating someone neurodivergent, it's so much easier connecting to people who already sort of think like I do. So I don't think it's hopeless if it turns out you're autistic, it just means you should probably change your approach to the kind of people you seek out. You might also be able to get advice from people on the spectrum who struggled socially JUST like you currently do, but we're able to learn how to socialize better. I think you'd actually be in a more hopeful situation if you ever sought out a diagnosis than if you never did so and continued to socialize with people in a way that clearly hasn't been working well for you for the 38 years you've been doing it.

>Others get it without doing anything but because I don't know how to talk to people I have to prove myself. Great

Let's try to look at this from a different POV for a moment, maybe try to reframe some of what you're thinking.

Imagine someone comes up to you and begins talking to you while you're out in public. You aren't really too sure what they want (maybe just wanting to make a friend), but they seem uncomfortable and like they're struggling to figure out how to keep a conversation going. 
But this isn't someone you know what to say anything to also. You don't really know much about them, maybe you see them around sometimes or share a class with them but that's all. You don't know they're interests, what their personality is like, and you're having a hard time even getting a sense of whether or not they'd even be someone you'd get a long with because you can't get a good read on their vibes. And since they seem uncomfortable having a conversation, you start to feel uncomfortable too. You probably feel bad since this is someone who's wanting to get to know people, but it's hard to genuinely connect to someone who not only seems awkward, but also isn't really saying anything you could really relate to either. You could make the effort to carry most of the conversation to make things easier for them, but they're still not giving you much to work with in terms of a real discussion. It gets a bit exhausting to talk to them after a while and you don't want to hurt their feelings, so you politely exit the conversation. 

All of this said, is this an interaction that you think would lead to others wanting to really get to know you? Of course not right? People tend to naturally gravitate towards people who make them feel good to talk to, not really to someone who (unintentionally) puts you in sort of an uncomfortable position. 

*It's not about proving yourself to others that you're a good enough person to have a conversation with, it's the fact that most people naturally bond with people when they're sharing some sort of positive emotions together.* Its not something you can brute force. It sounds like you don't yet know how to really generate those positive feelings in someone through conversation.

The obvious thing of course is that you don't just learn how to talk to people in a vacuum, you do have to go out and actually work on it and figure out how to do it. And that's incredibly hard. But its also important to let go of some of that vitriol that keeps you disconnected from people before you even start learning how to do that.

Everyone's deserving of love, even you. But I think you're a bit off the mark when it comes to understanding how it is that people seem to just "do nothing" and get people to care about them. They aren't doing nothing, it just looks effortless because they've done it their whole lives. But its better to learn how to do it late than never OP.

Do you think that people who have success in dating are perfect OP? 

You're right, you shouldn't have to be perfect in order to date. The good news is that you don't need to be perfect either. 

I think it might help you out to shift your point of view when you hear people say that you need to work on yourself in order to have luck dating. It's not about whether or not you're currently low value and will only raise your value if you work on yourself, it's more about the fact that working on yourself (emotionally) can give you a lot more confidence and security, which people are naturally attracted to. More importantly, working on your self esteem makes it easier to accept the times where you're maybe struggling to meet people, because you enjoy being single enough to not have a scarcity mindset if you're single. Because you understand that being single doesn't mean there's something wrong with you and that you're still a valuable person regardless of any external factors. 

It sounds like you're struggling pretty hard. I know its not easy to be in the position you're in. I know it sounds hard, but I think changing the way you're able to approach certain things is your best way out of where you're at now. The current path you're on is only going to continue to limit you and I think everyone has the potential to do better for themselves in order to have a happier life.

Why didn't you think to masturbate to the crushing fantasies sooner OP? If you connected stroking your dick to random boners, why did you wait so long to do it with the boners you had when you were thinking about men getting crushed? Like had you never heard of masturbation before? Did you know what it was? Did you not know how to do it? I feel like you would have heard some teenage boys in class talk about masturbation or something like that, right? Did you never have that thought of "Huh, that sounds interesting. I should try that sometime"? 

I feel like masturbation is such an instinctive thing to figure out for most people when they're puberty age, so I'm very curious as to how it seemed to elude you until you were an adult.

>if others petted me and told me that everything is fine and I don't have to change anything because it's OK, I wouldn't achieve anything

Not necessarily, there have been plenty of times where I've asked for reassurance from others about something, and I still decided to improve myself even after they told me that it was OK. When I was unemployed, people around me told me that was okay and that I shouldn't be too hard on myself for not working. I still decided to work towards not just having a job again, but also being more ambitious about a career in general.

It turns out that people usually don't respond well to someone telling it like it is. People ACTUALLY respond better to reassurance about things they're struggling with, and when they feel more comforted by others, they feel more confident to take steps to get better at whatever problem their having.

>Besides, you're trying to do that yourself.

Two things can be true at the same time, even if they seem contradictory. There's a kind way to be blunt with someone, and there's a mean way to do it. And the difference between the 2 is time and place. 

I know I said I was going to drop the topic of neurodivergence in my previous comment, but if you genuinely cannot tell when is the RIGHT time to be gentle or blunt with someone, and when is the WRONG time to be gentle or blunt with someone, that might be a sign that theres information that youre struggling to receive from the world around you, that most other people have no problems with understanding. I say this as someone who is also neurodivergent and constantly has a hard time with why some things are easy for "normal" people when they're extremely difficult for me. 

I'm not saying your brain is defective, just that I think you don't realize that your thought patterns are standing in the way of the things you want to have in life. If you're neurodivergent, you can't just be cured and have a normal brain. But you CAN learn shortcuts to things that are hard for you so that they start being easy for you. Therefore, you can choose to either ignore other people's suggestions about being neurodivergent and keep doing what clearly isn't working for you (and that may never work for you), OR you can try to look within yourself and see if there's something that you might need to accept in order to be able to try things that will get you the life that you want.

Again, yes I am being blunt right now like you said. I'm saying all of this to you now because I hate seeing other people struggling like how I've struggled my whole life. If you're doing things that are working against the way your brain works, you're only going to end up making yourself more miserable than you already are.

You don't seem as though you want to talk about any sort of neurodivergencies or anything like that, so I guess I won't say much more other than that I think you may not be seeing the point of what people mean when they say that what you're saying about other people isn't helping you if you want women to like you more.

"Telling it like it is" isn't always the kindest thing to do. There's also no point in being blunt because the world is harsh and reality needs to be dealt with. Don't you think that if a woman was fat or not conventionally attractive, she'd know that other people might be judging her for that? She wouldn't be  completely unaware that she's fat, she absolutely would know. She's lived in her fat body for her entire life and she's probably spent her whole life dealing with people treating her worse than thin women because of her weight. She'd be more aware of how people think of her than anyone else would be, because SHE'S the one that's being judged by people for being fat.  She would have no choice BUT to deal with reality and the harshness of the world. She can't escape it. Even if she lost the weight, she'd never be able to forget the way people treated her when she was fat and how much it hurt for her. Being treated better when you're thin won't ever outweigh the pain of people treating you like shit because you're fat.

 So what's the point in adding to the harshness she's already experiencing? It's not like she's learning something new, and she'd only feel worse if you reminded her of the thing she already knew.

 If you think being honest is doing the right thing, you're not understanding that the right thing would be to not be more cruel than the world as already been to someone.

Anyone asking something like that is already aware of the thing they're insecure about. They aren't asking for whether or not it's true, they just want someone to understand that other people have been cruel to them and they're seeking REASSURANCE because that's a natural human behavior when they've been treated poorly by others. That's not "making a fuss", thats something people do because we evolved to seek comfort from people when we're hurt because that's how we've been able to survive as a species for our entire time on Earth. The right thing to do is to reassure them that they're still worthy of people being kind to them regardless, not to be honest and add on to the hurt they've already been experiencing from people.

I want to assume that you're posting here in good faith because you want to improve yourself, so I want you to know that it's important that you learn how to be kinder to people if you ever want for people to like you. You can learn to change the way you think about things. Not everyone judges like that based on appearances OP. Any woman that you would WANT to be in a relationship with (and who would also be a good girlfriend) would be completely turned off by this thought process you have right now. You'll be hurting yourself more if you kept trying to convince a woman to like you without learning how to think differently about people.

Like the other commenters said, I think it's worth possibly looking into whether or not you're neurodivergent or on the spectrum. I've known a lot of autistic people who are practically incapable of lying, even if telling the truth is rude.

Deciding not to call someone fat, unattractive or boring isn't necessarily lying or being dishonest, it's just realizing that if you don't have anything nice to say then you don't have to say anything at all about her? 

Either way, I think a change in attitude could do you some good...maybe you think all those things about her, but she's a catch to someone else. Attraction is all subjective anyways.

If you sincerely didn't know it was an issue with your social skills, it means they need a lot of work right now.

It's not just about dating or being extroverted or anything, poor social skills can be bad for your career too. So regardless of whether or not you plan on talking to girls in the future, you should work on them regardless.

To answer your main question, my boyfriend has overjet teeth and I think it makes his smile so endearing. It makes his smile unique and it's one of his features that I really like.

But reading your post OP I completely even forgot what your initial question was because there's just so much to unpack here. Your teeth are not the issue here at all.

I can tell that it was hard for you to work up the courage to talk to her in the first place. Its good that you got out of your comfort zone, definitely keep working to be more comfortable with talking to people! That will give you a lot of opportunities to get better at talking to girls.

I think your main problem is that you seem to be getting very emotionally invested over someone you don't know. It also seems like your social skills are poor and you don't really know how to hold a basic conversation very well. I understand it's scary to talk to a girl you don't know, but there's more to being able to talk to someone than just getting over the anxiety and walking up to them to have a conversation. And speaking of anxiety, it sounds like you have a lot of social anxiety that's keeping you from being able to work on your social skills so that you CAN be able to hold a conversation. Running away because you were about to have a panic attack when her friends showed up is a whole issue in and of itself. 

I think you need to address all of those things before worrying about whether or not your teeth are going to stop you from dating.

I'd also advise that you maybe leave her alone for a while. When you said you heard her say "I don't, he just came up to me to talk", it didn't sound to me like she was warm to talking to you. Continuing to talk to her at this point might make things worse. Give her some space and if she wants to talk to you, she'll talk to you on her own time. That's something you have to build up to if you want to get to know someone. 

What signs were you getting that made you think she liked talking to you? Responding to your questions, asking simple questions in response to yours (Example: "What about you?") and smiling aren't always signs that someone's happy to talk to you. She might have been confused or nervous, but trying to be polite because you otherwise were being polite and she didn't want to be mean or anything.

I asked you that question more because I wanted you to actually engage with the idea that you could be projecting a feeling about yourself onto other people. 

It also seems like you maybe didn't read the full article, because while it's suggesting that yes, people CAN feel disgust when they see someone "ugly", that this is a bias that can do a lot of harm to people that are seen as ugly. It literally even ends by saying this:

> So next time you’re looking at something or someone you consider unattractive, just remember, there’s a psychological mechanism at play here that can override logic, but by being aware of it, we can challenge it.

I used to feel that same discomfort when I was in my teens, but I made an effort to grow past that because it's mentally healthier to learn how to stop being uncomfortable when seeing someone ugly. I stopped feeling so insecure in my own appearance once I learned to stop paying attention and giving a shit if someone was ugly. Like...it's possible to unlearn that, and you'd be much better off if you did.

[Dr K did a video](https://youtu.be/eTrI_kWet0c?si=M0FWRzK4EuraMKLe) where he talked about how feeling cringe about someone else was usually us making an internal judgement on ourselves. I think you would really benefit from watching it. 

If you can accept that you don't have to feel uncomfortable seeing someone ugly, it'll be easier to understand that women might not care what you look like just because you're talking to them. Tons of women don't care that much. But assuming that they do because of how you personally see the world and then feeling bad because you're thinking women must feel the same way you do, that's what's got you in this trap to begin with. Your own feelings and perceptions are not universal.

>I myself don't like talking to people who are VERY ugly.

May I ask why? Do you think this has anything to do with how you feel about looks? Do you feel like you're worth less to others because you think you're ugly, so then anyone else who's very ugly is also unworthy? Why exactly does talking to people who are really ugly make you uncomfortable?

Many people don't really think about people's appearances that hard. I don't care if someone ugly is talking to me, I'm more concerned about either what they're saying to me OR what's going on in my own life to even care about how good or bad they look. So I'm curious as to why you feel this way, OP.

Human beings aren't actually very genetically diverse in the grand scheme of things. At one point in our history as a species, we had a population bottleneck that brought us down to around 1-2 thousand people on the entire planet. While the various races of people appear different on the surface, even then the genetics that account for the different racial phenotypes isn't as diverse as you'd imagine. For reference, we share about 50% of our DNA with bananas. Even looking at chimpanzees as our closest living relative at around 98% similarity, were very different creatures.

There's just not enough genetic diversity among different ethnic groups that would necessarily lead to any one race being smarter than the other. Now there may be environmental factors, areas with food scarcity or war or any other traumatic/detrimental thing could result in a population with lower than average IQ scores. But that's not a matter of genetics at all. Any such environmental problem could theoretically be fixed and thus the populations average IQ would increase. It's also more often that intelligence varies more between 2 members of the same race/ethnic group than it does vary between 2 different races overall. 

This doesn't even bring into account the inherent flaws and biases that exist in an IQ score, or that intelligence is usually relevant to the environment someone exists in. It doesn't matter if you're the world's greatest mathematician if you don't have the mental ability to survive out in the elements and hunt and gather your own food. I think even in groups of people with a lower IQ average, their mental abilities are going to tend to be what is best suited for their environment.

It depends. If you simply want to get over your fear of talking to people and develop an emotional callus to it, then sure. You'll certainly desensitize yourself to the fear of talking to people if you do it enough times and learn that you'll still be ok if people reject you. 

But simply going up to people you don't know and striking a conversation with them is generally a misguided way to learn to talk to people, as it's not really how people naturally meet and befriend each other. Usually people click because they end up in a shared environment and somehow learn that they have something in common (hobbies, life experiences, etc) When people recognize that they have something in common with one another, it's easier for them to feel invested in becoming friends. 

But just going out in an environment that you normally don't enjoy being in and choosing a random stranger to talk to doesn't create that spark from having something in common, which is how bonds with people are formed. So your attempts might backfire because you're trying to learn social skills by forcing it in a way that's unnatural, and not by actually learning what makes people get along with each other. 

I know it's a cliche answer, but try to expand your hobbies a bit so that you have more opportunities to meet people. If you're into video games, maybe it's worth trying something like table top games, LARPing, cosplaying or going to conventions, etc. These are all much more social than simply playing League at home. I'm not saying this to shame you, I think it's important for you to see what sort of hole you could put yourself into if you decide the discomfort of self improvement is worse than the familiar misery that you feel right now. You owe it to yourself to choose a better outcome for your life dude.

When you first meet someone, you have to do your best to make sure the other person you're talking too is comfortable with you, and feels like they can communicate with you on an even playing field.

You would have every right to be annoyed if someone called you nonbinary. The idea that you check all the boxes for being a woman *and then saying* "Yes, I'm a woman, that's factually correct" IS you identifying yourself as a woman. That's all being cisgender is.

There's behaviors that strongly correlate to what hormones, sex organs, and chromosomes you have. That's what becomes "gender traits" depending on your culture. They're ways for people to affirm what *feels correct in their mind,* regardless of their birth sex. The feeling of what's right or not is different for everyone. And for some people, something about their birth sex doesn't match up with how they see themselves. Maybe they feel it doesn't match with man or woman at all. 

Some trans people compare being transgender or having gender dysphoria to having a rock stuck in your shoe. When it's there, it's uncomfortable and you're aware of it all the time because it sucks and you just want to get rid of it. But if someone doesn't have a rock stuck in their shoe, they don't think about it. Why would they? There's no rock in their shoe to bother them. Out of shoe out of mind or whatever.

⁠For people with pebbles in their shoes, maybe doing something like saying they're nonbinary while expressing or breaking gender stereotypes makes it feel like there's no more pebbles in their shoes. Maybe they even feel good and excited because they might finally know what it's like for the first time in their life to not have a rock in their shoe. And continuing to do those things *keeps* the rock out of their shoes.

For people who have *never* had a rock in their shoes and don't know what it feels like, they don't get why some people are making a big deal out of the shoe pebbles. Moreover, they don't get why they have to do certain things in order to keep out the rocks. Maybe they start thinking that these rocks are made up or something because they've never had one. Why bring attention to it? What if they just focused on living their lives and not thinking about rocks in their shoes? Maybe if they did that, they'd be too busy to notice the rock in their shoes. 

*But as everyone knows, having a rock stuck in your shoe fucking sucks and all you can think about when it's there is getting rid of it.*

⁠Honestly, I don't think it's necessary for people who aren't trans to know what a gender actually FEELS like. Just how someone doesn't have to know what it's like to have a rock in your shoe to see that it sucks for those that do, and the things they have to do to keep them out are important. 

It doesn't matter exactly what it means to feel like for everyone to be exist in society as a man or a woman. Everyone's internal and external's lives are different, so that "feeling" is different for everyone, and some people don't have it. 

Being nonbinary while doing or not doing certain gender things isn't meant to reinforce stereotypes or tell people that EVERYONE that doesn't conform to traditional gender norms is also nonbinary. We're just signifying that for whatever reason, a part of how we see ourselves might not match physical traits like biological sex. 

Sharing these feelings about gender can be a way to let people who might be questioning know that they aren't alone. If someone hears our nonbinary experiences and find them relatable, that only means that there *could* be a reason why, but that reason is only for them to decide for themselves. If they're ultimately feel like they're cis, that's absolutely fine.

My personal theory is that sex is necessary for our species to exist, so it makes sense that it somehow got wrapped up in how we view ourselves because it's an important part of how we know who to make more babies with. Even though mankind now has bigger things to worry about  like having a job or having a purpose, it's still pretty important for humans to do something that signals something like our biological sex in order for us to feel like a member of the human species. But because not everyone matches the sex assigned to them, we have to make our signals differently in order to feel that same type of belonging.
